## **Charging costs and infrastructure availability**

Charging cost is the biggest ongoing variable. Here is what each city's domestic tariff looks like:

* Delhi: [₹0.00/unit for the first 200 units](https://billunits.in/state-calculators/delhi-electricity-bill-calculator/), with the state government subsidising electricity for households consuming less than 200 units monthly. Between 201 and 400 units, the rate is ₹1.50/unit (50% subsidy on ₹3.00/unit).
* Bangalore: [Flat rate of ₹5.80/unit](https://billunits.in/state-calculators/bescom-bill-calculator/) for all consumption, though eligible households receive up to 200 free units under the Gruha Jyothi scheme
* Pune: [₹4.28/unit](https://billunits.in/state-calculators/msedcl-bill-calculator/) for the first 100 units, ₹11.10/unit for 101–300 units, plus 16% electricity duty
* Mumbai: Rates vary by distributor (Adani Electricity, Tata Power, BEST), [typically ranging from ₹3 to ₹9/unit](https://billunits.in/state-calculators/msedcl-bill-calculator/)

An electric scooter typically uses 2 to 4 units per full charge. In Delhi, if you stay within the free 200-unit threshold, your scooter charging cost is essentially zero. In Pune, a single charge under the higher slab costs ₹33-₹44.

VIDA EVooters offer flexibility here. All models support [three charging methods](https://www.vidaworld.com/charging-infrastructure.html): direct vehicle charge, removable battery at any standard 5A socket, and access to 5,900+ fast-charging stations across 450 cities. The shared charging socket (same for both the vehicle and the detached battery, no adaptor needed) means apartment dwellers can charge at home regardless of their parking setup.

## **Daily commuting patterns and EV economics**

Average [one-way commute distances](https://www.moveinsync.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/Travel-Time-Report.pdf) in these cities fall within a tight range: Delhi at 20 km, Bangalore at 19 km, Mumbai at 17 km, and Pune at 16 km. 

The practical takeaway: a 32-40 km daily round trip is the norm. Electric scooters with certified ranges above 90 km handle this comfortably on a single charge. For example, the [VIDA V2 Pro](https://www.vidaworld.com/vida-v2-pro.html) offers a 165 km IDC certified range, whereas even the more affordable [VIDA VX2 Go 2.2 kWh](https://www.vidaworld.com/vx2-go-electric-scooter.html) delivers 92 km. At a running cost of even less than half a rupee with home charging, the monthly expense for a 30 km daily commute will come to less than even ₹500.

## **Government policies and regional benefits**

Each state's EV policy adds distinct ownership advantages:

* Delhi (EV Policy 2026–2030): More than ₹3,900 crore allocated for greater EV adoption, with subsidies of ₹10,000 per kWh for electric two-wheelers priced up to ₹2.25 lakh in the first year. Full road tax and registration exemption.
* Karnataka (Clean Mobility Policy 2025–30): Targets [₹500 billion in clean mobility investments by 2030](https://www.mercomindia.com/karnatakas-clean-mobility-policy-2025-30-targets-%E2%82%B9500-billion-investment). Electric two-wheelers enjoy road tax and registration charge exemptions.
* Maharashtra (EV Policy 2025): [₹1,740 crore allocated for 1.75 lakh EVs](https://evreporter.com/maharashtra-electric-vehicle-policy-2025/), with charging stations mandated every 25 km on national and state highways. Toll exemptions on key expressways add value for Mumbai-Pune commuters.

For long-term cost certainty, VIDA, powered by Hero MotoCorp, includes a standard 5-year/50,000 km vehicle warranty and 3-year/30,000 km battery warranty. An opt-in [Extended Battery Warranty plan](https://www.vidaworld.com/battery-warranty.html) stretches battery coverage to 5 years/60,000 km, including degradation protection.

## **Which city offers the best value for EV owners?**

Delhi leads on paper, with the strongest combined subsidy stack and the cheapest electricity. With the draft policy officially finalised, a Delhi buyer can save up to ₹35,000 at purchase plus enjoy near-zero charging costs.

Mumbai and Pune offer solid mid-range value: ₹15,000 in combined subsidies and 100% road tax exemption.

Bangalore's electric scooter price benefits are limited to road tax exemption and the central subsidy, but the Gruha Jyothi free-units scheme can offset charging costs for eligible households.

For buyers seeking the lowest upfront cost, VIDA's [BaaS (Battery as a Service)](https://www.vidaworld.com/vx2-plus-electric-scooter.html) option on VX2 models separates the battery cost from the vehicle purchase, reducing the initial outlay across all four cities.

## **Conclusion**

The city you live in genuinely changes what you pay. Before comparing spec sheets, compare your state's subsidy structure and your electricity bill. To explore how specific models fit your budget and city, check out the full [VIDA scooter range](https://www.vidaworld.com/).

## **FAQs**

### **1. Does electric scooter pricing vary by city?**

Ex-showroom prices are typically uniform nationally. On-road prices differ because of state-level purchase subsidies, road tax policies, and registration fee exemptions.

### **2. Which city is best for electric scooter ownership?**

Delhi currently offers the strongest incentive combination: up to ₹35,000 in combined central and proposed state subsidies, 100% road tax exemption, and subsidised electricity with 200 free units monthly.

### **3. Are EV running costs different across cities?**

Yes, primarily due to electricity tariffs. Delhi's subsidised rates make charging nearly free for low-consumption households. Bangalore's flat rate of ₹5.80/unit is moderate. An electric scooter consumes roughly 2 to 4 units per full charge, so the per-charge cost ranges from near-zero in Delhi to approximately ₹20-25 in Maharashtra.

### **4. What affects electric scooter prices in India?**

The price of electric scooters in India depends on central PM E-DRIVE subsidies (₹2,500/kWh, capped at ₹5,000), state purchase incentives, road tax and registration exemptions, and GST (5% for EVs). Battery capacity, motor power, and features also influence the base price.

### **5. How does the PM E-DRIVE subsidy work for electric scooters?**

The PM E-DRIVE scheme offers ₹2,500 per kWh of battery capacity, capped at ₹5,000 per electric two-wheeler. It applies to vehicles with an ex-factory price of up to ₹1.5 lakh. The subsidy is available until July 31, 2026.

### **6. Is road tax exempted for electric scooters in all four cities?**

Yes. Delhi, Bangalore, Mumbai, and Pune all currently offer 100% exemptions on road tax and registration fees for electric two-wheelers. In Karnataka, this exemption applies specifically to electric two-wheelers under the Karnataka Motor Vehicles Taxation (Amendment) Act, 2026, even as electric cars now attract a 5–10% lifetime tax.

### **7. Can I charge an electric scooter at home in any of these cities?**

Yes. Most electric scooters can be charged using a standard 5A home socket. VIDA EVooters take this further with removable batteries that you can carry indoors and charge at any 5A socket, using the same shared charging socket that works on the vehicle. This is particularly useful in apartments without dedicated parking, common across all four cities.

Unagi, a San Francisco Bay Area-based electric scooter startup, will let you pay a monthly fee to hang onto the same scooter, a service that could solve a problem in the ride-sharing industry during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The company now offers two subscription plans as part of its Unagi All-Access service. The first is a pay-as-you-go $39-a-month plan and the second is a $408 annual subscription, which amounts to a $34 monthly fee. There's a one-time $50 setup fee for both plans, and insurance is included for if your scooter is stolen or damaged. However, there's an $85 deductible for a replacement scooter.

Customers who purchase the subscription will receive the company's Model One dual-motor scooter, which is priced at $990 to buy. A single motor vehicle is available for $840, though it's not apart of the subscription model. It has about 15 miles to a charge and takes about 5 hours to charge.

Unagi cofounder David Hyman told Business Insider that there are added perks of owning or renting one through a subscription vs accessing it only on the street, like not having to worry about the batteries running dead.

"Having one in your possession, when it's lightweight and portable, far exceeds a street scooter," Hyman said.

According to the company website, a team member will deliver your scooter to you for free within 24 hours after purchasing a subscription. The monthly payment service will roll out in Los Angeles as well as New York, a market that recently made it legal for electric scooters to operate on public streets. Unagi plans to roll out in more cities eventually.

Hyman said Unagi's subscription concept has been in the works since mid-2019, but "the timing is good" with the hypersensitivity to touch that has become a cultural mainstay during the pandemic. The health crisis has dealt a blow to the ride-sharing world — some people are less inclined to share a ride with a stranger or use a scooter or bike that had previously been used by someone else.

Hyman also said the company's scooter sales have surged in recent months.

"Before COVID, we were selling hundreds of scooters a month, and now we're selling thousands," Hyman said.

Unagi isn't the first e-scooter startup to test a subscription service. As The Verge notes, Bird did so in mid-2019, but Hyman said the issue with Bird's plan was that it used the scooters that were designed to live on the street in its subscription model, which made "no sense at all."

"It was an afterthought and not really a focused effort," Hyman said.

Unagi was founded in 2018 and, according to its Crunchbase profile, "aims to liberate people from the tyranny of transportation frustrations." The startup has raised $3.2 million in funding from investors, including Menlo Ventures.

As for the startup's name, Hyman said it is indeed in reference to the freshwater Japanese eel. The team settled on it while mulling over potential names that are associated with electricity.

# The Aspiration Gap: How India’s Electric Two-Wheeler Brands Are Racing to Win Urban Minds

Ken Research

August 21, 2026- 7min read

![Electric scooter market India](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fkenresearch.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fghost_blog%2Fghost_image%2Felectric-scooter-parked-outdoor-charging-station-with-city-stree_Sa29utC.webp&w=2048&q=75)

###### August 21, 2026

by Ken Research

## India’s Electric Two-Wheeler Market: A Race Defined by Aspiration, Not Just Adoption

India’s electric two-wheeler segment has crossed a threshold that no number alone can fully explain. Sales volumes surpassed **1 million units in FY2024**, and the segment is projected to reach **4.6 million units annually by FY2028**, expanding at a CAGR above 30%. Yet beneath the headline volumes lies a more commercially significant question: do consumers believe in the brands selling them these vehicles, or are they simply buying into a category? 

To answer this, Ken Research conducted its inaugural [**Electric Two-Wheeler Brand Perception & Urban Consumer Aspiration Survey**](https://www.kenresearch.com/survey/electric-two-wheeler-brand-perception-urban-consumer-aspiration-survey) across seven major cities, a study tracking the purchase intent, brand trust, and post-ownership sentiment of **3,900 active urban commuters and EV owners**. What emerged is not merely a consumer preference map. It is a diagnostic of the widening gap between what EV brands promise and what urban India experiences.

India’s top five electric two-wheeler brands collectively account for **over 78% of total EV two-wheeler sales**, yet brand loyalty, measured by repurchase intent and active recommendation, remains concentrated among a narrow segment of early adopters. **Charging infrastructure anxiety, after-sales uncertainty, and unresolved range concerns** continue to suppress conversion among the 63% of surveyed respondents who describe themselves as “EV-curious but uncommitted.” That gap is where the next decade of EV market leadership will be won or lost.

![Urban EV brand positioning by aspiration and accessibility](https://storage.ghost.io/c/a4/09/a4095af6-7105-4383-acb0-c4dc440fa896/content/images/2026/08/01-urban-ev-brand-positioning-matrix-clear.png)

Urban EV brand positioning by aspiration and accessibility

## Survey Profile: Who We Studied, Where, and Why It Matters

### Sample and Geography

The survey was conducted between Q1 and Q2 of 2025, covering a stratified, nationally representative sample of **3,900 urban commuters and active EV owners** across seven cities: **Delhi-NCR, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad,** **Chennai, Pune, and Ahmedabad**. These cities collectively account for approximately **72% of all registered electric two-wheelers** in India as of Q4 2024. Data was collected through a combination of online panels, EV dealership intercept interviews, and assisted digital surveys to ensure representation across ownership stages and digital access levels.

### Demographic Profile

* Age distribution: **41% Millennials (26–35)**, 27% Gen Z (18–25), 22% Gen X (36–45), 10% Boomers (46–60)
* Income brackets: **36% in the INR 6–12 lakh annual household income band**, 29% above INR 12 lakh, 35% in INR 3–6 lakh bracket
* EV ownership status: **44% current EV two-wheeler owners**; 38% active intenders within a 12-month purchase window; 18% early researchers
* Brand exposure breadth: **57% had test-ridden more than one EV brand**, with an average of 1.8 brands evaluated per active intender

![EV two-wheeler brand perception dimensions across leading brands](https://storage.ghost.io/c/a4/09/a4095af6-7105-4383-acb0-c4dc440fa896/content/images/2026/08/02-brand-perception-radar-ev-twowheeler-clear.png)

EV two-wheeler brand perception dimensions across leading brands

## The Brand Perception Divide: Where Urban Consumers Actually Place Their Trust

Over the past three years, India’s EV two-wheeler category has split into two distinct competitive layers, brands that have earned aspirational status among urban consumers, and brands that remain functionally relevant but aspirationally neutral. Our survey data reveals a **structurally significant divergence** in brand perception across design appeal, range confidence, and after-sales trust.

### What Urban Consumers Rate Highest, and Where Brands Are Falling Short

* **Design Appeal Leads Purchase Triggers at 71%:** Aesthetic design and perceived modernity rated as the primary purchase trigger among respondents aged 18–35, outranking running cost savings among this cohort for the first time in the survey. This shift signals that EV buying in India’s urban tier is becoming a **lifestyle statement**, not merely an economic calculation.
* **Range Anxiety Remains the Single Largest Barrier at 68%:** Despite technical improvements, 68% of EV-curious non-owners cited range uncertainty as their primary adoption barrier, with the perceived gap between advertised range and real-world performance being the specific source of distrust. **This is a communication failure as much as an engineering one.**
* **After-Sales Network Drives Brand Loyalty Depth:** Among current EV owners, after-sales service quality emerged as the strongest predictor of repurchase intent, with a satisfaction differential of 31 percentage points between high-rated and low-rated service experiences. Brands with smaller dealership networks are disproportionately penalised.
* **Government Subsidy Awareness Remains Low at 34%:** Only 34% of EV-intenders in the INR 3–6 lakh income bracket was aware of applicable state-level EV subsidies, a market education gap that is actively suppressing conversion in the most price-sensitive segment.

The result: **India’s urban EV two-wheeler market is bifurcating. Brands that have built design credibility and service depth are compounding loyalty among early adopters. Brands that have not are competing on** **price and** **discovering that price alone cannot sustain market share in a category where consumer expectations are rising quarterly.**

![EV purchase intent drivers across income segments](https://storage.ghost.io/c/a4/09/a4095af6-7105-4383-acb0-c4dc440fa896/content/images/2026/08/03-ev-purchase-intent-income-segments-clear.png)

****EV purchase intent drivers across income segments****

## The Ownership Reality: A Market Shaped by Unmet Expectations, Not Just Enthusiasm

If brand perception reveals what urban consumers hope to experience, post-purchase sentiment reveals how sharply those hopes are tested. Our survey identified the **expectation-to-reality gap** as the most commercially consequential data point in the dataset, more predictive of brand switching and negative word-of-mouth than price dissatisfaction or product failure alone.

### The Urban EV Ownership Reckoning

* **Range Perception Gap Averages 28 Percentage Points:** 89% of pre-purchase respondents expected their chosen EV to meet their daily commute needs without charging anxiety. Only 61% of post-purchase owners reported this expectation being consistently met in real-world conditions, a 28-point perception gap that drives 43% of negative brand reviews.
* **Public Charging Infrastructure Scores 48% Satisfaction Among Owners:** Access to reliable public charging was rated positively by only 48% of surveyed EV owners across the six cities, with Delhi-NCR and Hyderabad recording the highest dissatisfaction at 78% and 74% respectively. Infrastructure deficit is translating directly into brand blame.
* **Resale Value Uncertainty Depresses Premium Segment Growth:** Only 45% of surveyed EV owners felt confident about their vehicle’s resale value after 3 years, a figure that falls to 31% among buyers of brands launched after 2022. Resale uncertainty is creating a ceiling on willingness-to-pay for premium EV variants, constraining brands’ ability to exit the mid-segment.

What Brands Must Confront: Unlike petrol two-wheeler markets, where product reliability is largely a solved problem, [**India’s EV two-wheeler brands are selling a category still building its proof base**](https://www.kenresearch.com/industry-reports/india-electric-two-wheeler-market)**.** The brands that close the expectation gap, through transparent range communication, service network density, and resale value guarantees, will define the loyalty architecture of the market. Those that do not will find churn rising as the market matures and switching costs fall.

![EV ownership reality gaps across post-purchase factors](https://storage.ghost.io/c/a4/09/a4095af6-7105-4383-acb0-c4dc440fa896/content/images/2026/08/04-ev-expectation-vs-ownership-reality-clear.png)

****EV ownership reality gaps across post-purchase factors****

## What Lies Ahead: The Strategic Reckoning for India’s EV Two-Wheeler Brands

The rise of design-driven, aspiration-led EV purchasing in India’s urban centres has triggered more than a product development challenge, it has forced a fundamental brand-building reckoning for OEMs, charge-point operators, and policymakers alike. What worked to drive early adoption, government incentive messaging, fuel savings arithmetic, and novelty positioning, is no longer sufficient in a market that is maturing faster, comparing more carefully, and choosing with growing commercial sophistication.

Brands must now confront hard strategic questions:

**Do they invest in after-sales network depth, or continue to prioritise sales velocity at the expense of service quality?**

**Do they treat range anxiety as a product engineering problem, or as a communication and trust architecture challenge?**

**Do they design for the aspirational urban early adopter, or architect product variants and financing for the INR 3–6 lakh commuter segment that** **represents** **62% of two-wheeler volume?**

Deploying uniform brand positioning without income-tier and city-level segmentation is no longer viable. India’s EV consumer is evolving, and so is the definition of what brand trust means in a category with a 28-point expectation gap.

Challenger brands have demonstrated that loyalty in the EV space does not require decades of brand history, it requires **range transparency, service presence, and a community of advocates who close the credibility gap that advertising cannot.**

![Indian city EV adoption barriers anxiety heatmap](https://storage.ghost.io/c/a4/09/a4095af6-7105-4383-acb0-c4dc440fa896/content/images/2026/08/05-urban-anxiety-heatmap-ev-adoption-clear.png)

Indian city EV adoption barriers anxiety heatmap

### About the Author

[**Ayush Mathur**](http://linkedin.com/in/ruhtamhsuya/) is a survey research analyst at Ken Research, specialising in market research and data-driven decision-making. He works with organisations to bridge the gap between primary data and strategic insight, with hands-on experience designing and analysing large-scale consumer surveys across multiple sectors and geographies.

### From the Author

"At Ken Research, we set out to measure enthusiasm and ended up measuring trust deficit instead. The data is consistent and confronting: India's urban EV two-wheeler buyer isn't short on aspiration, 71% are choosing on design and lifestyle appeal before they even get to running costs. But that aspiration is colliding with a 28-point gap between what buyers expect and what they experience after purchase. This is not a demand problem. It is a credibility problem, and credibility isn't built through subsidy messaging or novelty positioning. It is built through range transparency, service network depth, and brands willing to be measured by what happens after the sale, not just at the point of it. Until OEMs can close that gap with evidence rather than advertising, the market will keep converting curiosity into ownership more slowly than its volume numbers suggest."

### About Ken Research

Ken Research is a market intelligence and strategy consulting firm delivering actionable insights across the various sectors in dynamic markets. We support industry stakeholders with data-driven analysis on emerging trends, competitive benchmarking, pricing strategies, and shifting consumer preferences. E-bikes and scooters being littered around major European cities have become a common sight over the last five years, as startups pitch themselves as a solution to transport's "last-mile" problem.

A few companies are emerging as the leaders in the micromobility sector, an umbrella term that largely refers to small, electric vehicles that tend to be lightweight and are unable to travel faster than 25 miles per hour.

Companies like Lime, Dott, Bolt, and Bird have expanded as Europeans gravitated toward the new form of transport. Their business model centers around rental, where users can pick up a scooter or bike from a location, use an app to unlock it for a fee before returning it to a specific parking site.

Millions of users are also opting to buy their own micro vehicles. In Europe, direct-to-consumer (D2C) e-bike sales are set to reach 17 million units sold annually by 2030, up from 3.7 million in 2019, meaning that despite their steep price, consumers are keen on less pedaling and more power.

The next iteration on the business model looks to be subscriptions, where users pay a monthly fee to access scooters or bikes.

Sweden's Vässla, Germany's Dance, Bloom in France, and Dutch startup Swapfiets have all raised funding to wean Europeans off buying or renting scooters and bikes.

"We're addressing the next generation of consumers through a subscription model because it's more convenient not to own things," Rickard Bröms, the CEO of Vässla, told Insider.

"It's better for customers because they avoid the major payment hurdle of spending thousands on a bike. It's a generalization, but the rise of Netflix and other services means that subscriptions are a trend that's here to stay."

Subscribing to a branded e-bike costs around $85 a month, including servicing and repairs.

Whether users want to add yet another subscription service to the growing pile is still to be tested, but the pitch is that it could be a cheaper alternative to car ownership, or buying an electric car.

Investors are seeing dollar signs. Subscription startups can be more attractive to venture capitalists than hardware businesses, because investors see annual recurring revenue, which VCs prefer as a method of valuing and appraising tech businesses.

"Subscriptions solve a lot of the pain points we see in micromobility," said Raphael Cattan, associate at French investor Eurazeo, which has backed Dance. "We think that e-bikes will make up a significant part of the market going forward but they are expensive to buy and maintain, there are few repair shops, and you also need insurance."

By managing a fleet of leased vehicles, startups in the space hope to be able to maximize both the usage and lifetime of their products through tech such as GPS, Internet of Things, and vehicle monitoring.

Vässla has expanded beyond its native Sweden for Madrid, Berlin, and Vienna, while Swapfiets has launched in London and a number of French cities including Paris.
